newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Kmart to pay off term loan by June.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kmart to pay off term loan by June.

text.p: Kmart Corp., which raised $331.7 million in a real estate refinancing deal on Wednesday, expects to pay off the remainder of a $1.2 billion term loan within the next 60 to 90 days, Kmart vice president and treasurer Michael Viola said.
Viola told Reuters in an interview that with Wednesday's transaction complete, Kmart has now paid off about $950 million of the bank term loan.
The loan was taken on last year as part of a debt restructuring that helped avert a financial crisis for the nation's third largest retailer.
Viola said the repayment of the term loan was a necessary step for Kmart to improve its credit rating, which was cut below investment grade at the end of 1995.
"One of the financial goals is to get back to an investment grade credit rating," Viola said, adding that Kmart needs to further improve operating results to achieve that goal.
The real estate sale-lease back deal will allow Kmart to cut its interest costs by about $7 million annually, Viola said.

Under the transaction, Kmart put about 81 store properties into a wholly owned real estate trust, which issued $335 million in commercial mortgage-backed securities and sold them in private placements to institutional investors. Kmart has signed long-term leases on the stores with the trust.

The average coupon on the floating rate securities is the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) plus 47 basis points. That compares to LIBOR plus 250 basis points for the term loan debt, resulting in a reduction of more than two full percentage points.

The remaining $250 million of the term loan will likely be paid off with proceeds from several sources, including $74.25 million in cash from the sale of Kmart's interest in its Mexican retail operations and future store sale leaseback deals and operating cash flow.
Viola noted that Kmart's free cash flow -- net operating cash flow minus capital expenditures -- improved by more than $1 billion during fiscal 1996 from fiscal 1995.
He said it was not likely that Kmart would continue to pay down debt as aggressively once the term loan is paid off. The company issued about $1 billion in convertible preferred shares last year.

"If we start to accumulate cash in a big way, we may go out to the market to buy back debt," he said. "But you'd have to be talking about hundreds of millions of dollars of idle cash that will be around for a long time"

Instead, Kmart plans to harness its improved cash flow to boost capital expenditures on store refurbishments and development. The company has said it will increase store spending to about $700 million in fiscal 1997 from $343 million in 1996.
